## <span class="dot dot-warning"></span> Watch Out — Starting Fresh? Run This First
If you're jumping into this module on a new day, or `raw_data` and
`raw_metadata` aren't in your environment, run this once before continuing:

```{r}
#| eval: false
library(tidyverse)
library(here)
library(janitor)

metadata_url  <- "https://raw.githubusercontent.com/CWML/ARCS/main/data/GSE113754_filtered_metadata.csv"
rawcounts_url <- "https://raw.githubusercontent.com/CWML/ARCS/main/data/GSE113754_GeneLevel_Raw_data.csv"

download.file(metadata_url,  destfile = here("raw_data", "GSE113754_filtered_metadata.csv"))
download.file(rawcounts_url, destfile = here("raw_data", "GSE113754_GeneLevel_Raw_data.csv"))

raw_metadata <- read_csv(here("raw_data", "GSE113754_filtered_metadata.csv"))
raw_data     <- read_csv(here("raw_data", "GSE113754_GeneLevel_Raw_data.csv"))
```
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## <span class="dot dot-live"></span> Browser Only Version — Load Straight From the URL
No persistent filesystem here, so skip the download step and read
directly from the source instead:

```{webr-r}
library(dplyr)
library(tidyr)
library(stringr)
library(janitor)
library(readr)

raw_metadata <- read_csv("https://raw.githubusercontent.com/CWML/ARCS/main/data/GSE113754_filtered_metadata.csv")
raw_data     <- read_csv("https://raw.githubusercontent.com/CWML/ARCS/main/data/GSE113754_GeneLevel_Raw_data.csv")
```
:::

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## <span class="dot dot-tip"></span> Learn More — The `rio` Package
`rio::import()` is a popular alternative that auto-detects file type and
picks the right reader underneath — handy if your project mixes `.csv`,
`.xlsx`, `.sav`, and `.dta` files. For a single, consistent file type like
the `.csv` files here, `read_csv()` works directly and is what you'll see
most often in published scripts and tutorials.
:::

## Cleaning the Raw Counts with `dplyr` Verbs and the Pipe

```{webr-r}
clean_data <- raw_data %>%
  clean_names() %>%
  rename(gene_id = v1) %>%
  mutate(gsm3119015 = replace_na(gsm3119015, 0)) %>%
  mutate(gene_id_symbol = paste(gene_id, gene_symbol, sep = "|")) %>%
  select(gene_id_symbol, everything(), -gene_symbol, -gene_id) %>%
  column_to_rownames(var = colnames(.)[1])
```

## Cleaning the Metadata

```{webr-r}
clean_meta_data <- raw_metadata %>%
  clean_names() %>%
  rename(sample_id = v1, condition = characteristics) %>%
  mutate(
    condition = case_when(
      grepl("homecage", condition)          ~ "normal",
      grepl("sleep deprivation", condition) ~ "sleep_deprived",
      TRUE ~ condition
    )) %>%
  mutate(
    genotype = case_when(
      grepl("WT",     genotype, ignore.case = TRUE) ~ "WT",
      grepl("shank3", genotype, ignore.case = TRUE) ~ "shank3",
      TRUE ~ genotype
    )) %>%
  mutate(geno_cond = paste0(genotype, condition)) %>%
  select(sample_id, genotype, condition, geno_cond) %>%
  mutate(sample_id = str_to_lower(sample_id))
```

## Harmonizing the Two Files

```{webr-r}
clean_data <- clean_data %>%
  select(all_of(clean_meta_data$sample_id))

setequal(clean_meta_data$sample_id, colnames(clean_data))
```

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## <span class="dot dot-note"></span> About This — This Is the Whole Point
This check is exactly what the Arc 2 "data management gone awry" story
was missing — a scripted, verifiable confirmation that two files
actually match, instead of a manual check done from memory.
:::

## What We Did, and Why

**What we built:** imported both raw files with `read_csv()`, cleaned the
counts matrix and the metadata separately using `dplyr`/`janitor` verbs
chained with the pipe, and ended with a scripted check confirming the two
cleaned files actually line up with each other.

**Why it matters:** every step here replaces something that could have
been done by hand, in a spreadsheet, invisibly — renaming a column,
recoding a label, matching sample IDs by eye. Writing it as code instead
means the exact same cleaning happens the same way every time, and the
final `setequal()` check turns "I'm pretty sure these match" into
something you can actually verify, instead of trust.
